# goal.js: all the docs

> Every page of https://goallabs.github.io/goal, in one file. The short index is https://goallabs.github.io/goal/llms.txt.

# goal.js

A compiled JavaScript framework where **`var` is state** and **`let`/`const` are computed**.

- **Server-rendered and resumable.** Pages are rendered on the server, and the browser resumes them
  instead of hydrating: no component code runs at load.
- **Small.** Each component's code loads on its first event, in a chunk of its own: 220 B to 1.3 kB
  gzipped in the demo app. A page with no events ships no JavaScript at all.
- **One source, the same rules on the server and in the browser.** Each `.goal` file compiles once
  into the server's code and the browser's, from the same templates, with the same escaping and URL
  checks. What the browser renders always agrees with what the server sent. See
  [How it works](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/how-it-works#one-source-for-the-server-and-the-browser).
- **No `async`, no `fetch`.** Components reach the server through [server functions](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/server-functions),
  called like plain functions.
- **Secure by default.** Escaping, URL checks, a strict Content-Security-Policy, CSRF protection and
  safe cookies are on with no setup. Each one has an explicit way out. See [Security](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security).
- **HTML as written.** Events are `onclick`, attributes are `class` and `for`, and `{if}` goes straight
  in the markup. There is no `bind:`, `@`, `:` or `$`.

```jsx
// app.goal
import { Counter } from './Counter.goal';

route GET / {
  return <main><h1>Hello</h1><Counter start={1} /></main>;
}
```

```jsx
// Counter.goal
export function Counter({ start }) {
  var count = start;                         // state
  const double = count * 2;                  // computed

  return (
    <div>
      <button onclick={() => count++}>+</button>
      <p>{double}</p>
      {if (count > 9) <b>big</b> else <span>small</span>}
    </div>
  );
}
```

- [Getting started](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/getting-started): install goal.js and run your first app.

- [Server functions](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/server-functions): calling the server from a component.
- [Types](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/types): `#strict` files, checked before the app runs.
- [Security](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security): what is on by default, and how to change it.
- [How it works](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/how-it-works): parse, compile, render and resume, and debugging.
- [Performance](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/performance): benchmark results, and how to measure your own.
- [Vite](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/vite): working on an app inside Vite's dev server.
- [Tools](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/tools): `goal add` sets up Tailwind CSS, Prisma, Drizzle, ESLint, Prettier, Vitest,
  Playwright and Sentry.
- For AI assistants: [llms.txt](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/llms.txt), a summary of goal.js with a
  link to each page, and [llms-full.txt](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/llms-full.txt), all the docs
  in one file.

## Status

goal.js is young, and these are not supported yet:

- components inside a keyed list's row.

# Getting started

## Install

goal.js needs Node.js. Make a folder for your app and install it there:

```bash
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
npm init -y
npm install goaljs
```

## Your first app

An app is a folder of `.goal` files. Create `app.goal`:

```jsx
import { Counter } from './Counter.goal';

route GET / {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <head>
        <meta charset="utf-8" />
        <title>My app</title>
      </head>
      <body>
        <h1>Hello</h1>
        <Counter start={1} />
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

And `Counter.goal`:

```jsx
export function Counter({ start }) {
  var count = start;
  return <button onclick={() => count++}>Clicked {count} times</button>;
}
```

Then start the development server:

```bash
npx goal dev .
```

Open <http://localhost:5648> and click the button. The page was rendered on the server; the
component's code loaded when you pointed at the button, and the click updated only the number.

Now change `Counter.goal`, say the button's text, and save. The page updates without reloading, and
the count stays where it was. A stylesheet change applies in place, and a compile error shows over
the page, with the file, line and column, until you fix it.

## Commands

```bash
goal dev <app>      # build, serve with error details, update open pages when a file changes
goal build <app>    # compile into <app>/dist; prints the routes and each chunk's size
goal start <app>    # serve a built app (--port 5648)
goal check <app>    # check every file, types too, and list the errors
goal add <tool>     # set up Tailwind CSS, Prisma, ESLint, Vitest and more (see Tools)
```

## What goes in an app

- `.goal` files, anywhere in the folder: [routes](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/routes) and [components](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/components), each with
  its own CSS in a [style block](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/components#styles) if it likes.
- `.js` and `.json` files for server code the `.goal` files import.
- A `public/` folder for CSS, images and fonts, served as they are. With a `postcss.config.js`, the
  stylesheets go through PostCSS first (see [Tools](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/tools)).
- An optional `goal.config.js` that changes the [security defaults](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security) and can report
  [errors](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security#errors).
- An optional `.env` file, read into `process.env` by `goal dev` and `goal start`. A variable that's
  already set in the environment wins.

Other folders are fine too: `goal build` skips `node_modules` and `dist`.

# Routes

```jsx
route GET /notes { ... }
route POST /notes { ... }
route GET /users/{id}/posts/{post} { ... }
```

A route is written at the top level of any `.goal` file. It has a method (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`,
`PATCH` or `DELETE`), a path where `{name}` is a parameter, and a body that runs on the server once
per request. The body may use `await`.

## In the body

- Path parameters are plain variables (`id`, `post`), as strings. They're constants: give a new value
  a name of its own (`const n = Number(id)`).
- `request` has `method`, `path`, `url`, `params`, `query`, `headers`, `cookies`, `form` (a form's
  fields), `files` (a form's files), `json` (a JSON body) and `signal`, an AbortSignal that's aborted
  when the client goes away.
- `cookie(name, value, options)` sets a cookie.

## What a route returns

| Return | Response |
|---|---|
| Markup | An HTML page |
| `redirect('/path')` | 303 to that path, on this site only; `redirect(url, { external: true })` to leave it |
| `json(value, status, headers)` | JSON |
| `reply(body, { status, type, headers })` | Markup as a page, text, or bytes (a Buffer), with any status and headers |
| `stream(source, { status, type, headers })` | Each piece an async generator gives, sent as it comes |
| `events(source, { ping, headers })` | Server-sent events: each value the source gives, as JSON |
| `notFound()` | 404 |
| Nothing | 204 |

The security headers stay on every answer; a header passed to `reply()` or the others replaces one of
them only when it has the same name.

## Streams and server-sent events

`stream()` sends a big answer a piece at a time, waiting while the client catches up. It stops when
the client goes away, and `request.signal` tells a slow source the same:

```jsx
route GET /export.csv {
  return stream((async function* () {
    yield 'id,title\n';
    for await (const n of notes(request.signal)) yield `${n.id},${n.title}\n`;
  })(), { type: 'text/csv' });
}
```

`events()` answers an `EventSource`. Each value is one message, as JSON, and a comment every `ping`
milliseconds (15 seconds by default) keeps the connection open through proxies:

```jsx
route GET /clock {
  return events((async function* () {
    while (!request.signal.aborted) {
      yield { now: Date.now() };
      await new Promise((ok) => setTimeout(ok, 1000));
    }
  })());
}
```

```js
new EventSource('/clock').onmessage = (e) => console.log(JSON.parse(e.data).now);
```

An error in the middle of a stream is logged and cuts the answer short, since its status is already
sent.

Markup that starts with `<html>` is the whole document: put `<title>` and
`<link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css" />` in its `<head>`. Other markup goes in a plain document.

## Groups

A group puts routes under one path. Its `before` block runs before each of them, and one that
returns something answers the request in the route's place:

```jsx
group /admin {
  before {
    const user = await session(request.cookies.sid);
    if (!user?.admin) return redirect('/login');
    request.user = user;
  }

  route GET / { return <main><Dashboard user={request.user} /></main>; }
  route GET /users/{id} { return <main><User id={id} /></main>; }
}
```

These answer `/admin` and `/admin/users/{id}`. Groups can hold groups: the outer `before` runs first,
and a path parameter of a group's path is a constant in every block inside it. A group has at most
one `before`.

## API routes

A group written `group /path api` answers other programs: a mobile app, another server, a webhook,
or a page on another site. Its routes, and those of the groups inside it, work differently:

- **No CSRF check.** Cookies are neither read nor set (`request.cookies` is empty and `cookie()`
  throws), so a request from another site carries nothing it could misuse. Check a token from a
  header, such as `Authorization`, in `before`.
- **Any body.** JSON still arrives in `request.json`, and every body is in `request.body` as bytes
  (a Buffer), say to check a webhook's signature.
- **Errors as JSON**, like `{ "error": "Not found" }`, `notFound()` included.
- **Other sites' pages may read the answers only when allowed**, with *config* `cors` in
  `goal.config.js`: a list of origins, or `'*'` for any. Preflight `OPTIONS` requests are answered
  for you.

```jsx
group /api/v1 api {
  before {
    const user = await userFromToken(request.headers.authorization);
    if (!user) return json({ error: 'sign in' }, 401);
    request.user = user;
  }

  route GET /notes { return json(await notes(request.user)); }
  route POST /notes { return json(await addNote(request.user, request.json), 201); }
}
```

```js
// goal.config.js
export default { cors: ['https://app.example.com'] };
```

## Matching

- Fixed paths win over paths with parameters: `/users/new` is chosen before `/users/{id}`.
- A path with the wrong method gets 405, with an `Allow` header.
- HEAD works wherever GET does.

## File uploads

A form with `enctype="multipart/form-data"` sends its files. Its text fields arrive in `request.form`,
and each file input's files in `request.files`, as a list under the input's name. A file is
`{ name, type, size, data }`, where `data` is a Buffer:

```jsx
<form method="post" action="/photos" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="photo" multiple />
  <button>Upload</button>
</form>
```

```jsx
route POST /photos {
  for (const f of request.files.photo ?? []) save(f.data);
  return redirect('/photos');
}
```

The file name and type come from the browser, so don't use them as a path or trust them. A file input
left empty arrives as an empty field. The whole body is limited to 1 MB by default: raise
[`bodyLimit`](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security#the-rest) for bigger files.

## Forms with any method

A form can use any method. `<form method="delete" action="/notes">` is sent as a POST with the method
in a hidden field, and the route for `DELETE /notes` answers it. Forms that send data get the
[CSRF token](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security#csrf) automatically.

# Components

```jsx
export function Counter({ start }) {
  var count = start;                         // state
  const double = count * 2;                  // computed
  const tone = count % 2 ? 'odd' : 'even';   // computed

  return (
    <div class={tone}>
      <button onclick={() => count++}>+</button>
      <p>{double}</p>
      {if (count > 9) <b>big</b> else if (count < 0) <i>negative</i> else <span>small</span>}
    </div>
  );
}
```

A component is a top-level function with a capitalised name that ends in `return <element>`: one
element, not a fragment, and no other `return`. It takes at most one parameter, its props.

## State and computed values

- **`var`** declares state, one name at a time, at the top of the component. A `var` anywhere else in
  a component, in a block or inside a function such as an event handler, is an error, so a `var` is
  always state. Inside a function, `let` and `const` are ordinary local variables.
- State changes only in event handlers (`count++`, `count = x`), never while rendering.
- Replace arrays and objects instead of changing them in place: `items = [...items, x]`. A change is
  seen when the variable is assigned.
- **`let` and `const`** are computed: they are worked out again from state each time. A `let` can be
  set by `if`/`else` while rendering, but a handler can't change it. The compiler says to use `var`.
- A handler can't change a prop either: copy it into state (`var count = start`) and change that.
- A component can't change a variable declared outside it, at the top of the file: no page would
  update, and on the server every request shares it. Routes and server functions can.
- A `const` or an import that's assigned is an error when the app compiles, not when the code runs.
- The component body runs again on every update, so it must be pure: no side effects while rendering.

## Markup

- **`{if (a) X else if (b) Y else Z}`** and ternaries go straight in markup, and in attribute values.
  Without an `else`, nothing is rendered.
- **HTML names.** Events are `onclick`, `oninput`, `onsubmit` and so on, with a function. Attributes are
  `class`, `for`, `disabled`, `value`. A reactive attribute is just `name={expression}`.
- A form with `onsubmit` never reloads the page.
- `{value}` children are escaped. `null`, `false` and `true` render nothing, and arrays are joined.
- When a `{...}` hole changes, its new markup goes into the nodes already there: an element that is
  still the same kind of element is kept, so an input inside the hole keeps its focus and what was
  typed.

## Lists

Event handlers work anywhere in the markup, including on list items:

```jsx
<ul>{items.map((x) => <li onclick={() => (picked = x)}>{x}</li>)}</ul>
```

A list without keys is made again as a whole when it changes, which is fine for a short one.

### Keyed lists

`key` on a list's rows patches the list by key:

```jsx
<ul>{items.map((x) => <li key={x.id}>{x.text}</li>)}</ul>
```

When the list changes, a kept row gets only its changed values written, new rows are added in one go,
and only the rows that are out of order move. Only a component with a keyed list loads that code.

A keyed list can go anywhere in the markup: straight in it, in an `{if}` or ternary branch, inside
an element in a branch, or inside another list's row.

```jsx
<ul>{if (open) items.map((x) => <li key={x.id}>{x.text}</li>) else <li>Closed</li>}</ul>
```

Inside an element in a branch, or in a row, the rows carry their key. When the markup around them
changes, each row is found by its key and moved, keeping its nodes, and with them an input's focus
and what was typed.

A list that never changes, such as one in a route, renders once and needs no key.

## Components inside components

A component can render another anywhere in its markup: in its fixed part, in an `{if}` or ternary
branch, or in a list without keys.

```jsx
export function Panel() {
  var open = true;
  var n = 1;
  return (
    <div>
      <button onclick={() => n++}>more</button>
      {if (open) <Counter start={n} />}
      <Counter start={n} />
    </div>
  );
}
```

- When the props a child gets read state, the child is rendered again in the browser when they change.
  It keeps its own state, so the second `Counter` above shows the new `start` and keeps its count.
- A component in a `{...}` hole starts from its props when it appears, and keeps its state while it
  stays. Each one keeps its own, even next to others of its kind. In a keyed list's rows, each keeps
  its state by its row's key, so the components of a row that moves move with it.
- A child without state or handlers ships no code of its own: its parent renders it again.

To render a child in the browser, the parent's code includes the child's template, and the module code
it uses, but nothing else from the child's file: routes and server functions stay on the server.

### Children

Markup between a component's tags is its `children`:

```jsx
<Card title="Total"><p>{count}</p><button onclick={() => count++}>+</button></Card>
```

```jsx
export function Card({ title, children }) {
  return <section><h2>{title}</h2>{children}</section>;
}
```

Children belong to the component that wrote them: `{count}` and the `onclick` above are the parent's,
wherever `Card` puts them. Put `{children}` in the child's fixed part, not inside a `{...}` hole that
renders again: that would be a compile error.

### Function props

A function passed as a prop runs in the component that passed it:

```jsx
<Picker onpick={(x) => (picked = x)} />
```

```jsx
export function Picker({ onpick }) {
  var n = 0;
  return <button onclick={() => onpick(++n)}>pick</button>;
}
```

When `Picker` calls `onpick`, the parent's state changes and the parent updates, as if it had handled
an event itself. Call a function prop from an event handler, not while rendering: on the server it does
nothing.

## Styles

A `style` block holds a file's CSS. It styles only the markup that file renders:

```jsx
style {
  .card { border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 8px; }
  strong { color: #1d4ed8; }
}

export function Counter({ start = 0 }) {
  var count = start;
  return <div class="card"><strong>{count}</strong></div>;
}
```

- Each element the file renders carries the file's scope, an attribute like `g-x7k2pq`, and each
  selector gets it on its last part: `.card strong` styles a `<strong>` this file renders, inside any
  `.card`. The scope adds no specificity, so a selector weighs what it does as written.
- Markup given to a component as children belongs to the file that writes it, and so do its styles.
  A parent styles what it passes in; the child styles its own markup.
- Rules inside `@media`, `@supports`, `@container` and `@layer` are scoped too, and so are nested
  rules. `@keyframes` and `@font-face` are kept as written, and their names are the page's.
- A file has one style block, at its top level. `@import` doesn't go in one: put page-wide CSS in a
  stylesheet under `public/` and link it.
- `goal build` puts every file's style block in one stylesheet, `/c/_/style.css`, and each page links
  it at the end of its head, after the page's own stylesheets. With a `postcss.config.js`, it goes
  through PostCSS too. There is no inline style, so the strict Content-Security-Policy stays.

## Compile errors

Breaking a rule is a compile error with the file, line and column:

```
components/Counter.goal:6:3: `count` is state: change it in an event handler, not while rendering
components/Counter.goal:9:15: write onclick, the HTML name, not onClick
```

## Not supported yet

- Components inside a keyed list's row.

# Server functions

```jsx
// notes.goal
const notes = [];

export server function addNote(text) {
  notes.push(String(text).slice(0, 200));
  return notes;
}

export function Notes() {
  var list = [];
  var saving = false;

  function add(e) {
    saving = true;              // shown at once
    list = addNote('hello');    // a request to the server; the handler waits for the answer
    saving = false;
  }

  return <button onclick={add} disabled={saving}>Add ({list.length})</button>;
}
```

A `server function` runs on the server. A component calls it like any other function, from an event
handler or from a function declared at the top of the component, and goal.js sends the request and
waits for the answer.

Nobody writes `async`, `await` or `fetch`: in a component they are compile errors. The page updates as
soon as the handler changes something (`saving = true` above), and again when the server answers.
Routes and other server functions call server functions directly, also with no `await`.

## Rules

- Arguments and the return value travel as JSON, so dates, maps and class instances don't arrive as
  they were.
- Each server function is a `POST /_m/<file>/<name>` endpoint behind the [CSRF check](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security#csrf);
  the page carries the token. Treat its arguments as untrusted input.
- A component can't call one while rendering, except through [`call()`](#loading-data-with-call).
  Otherwise, load the data in the route and pass it as a prop.
- Server functions are declared at the top level of a file. `export server function` lets other
  `.goal` files import them.

## Loading data with call()

`call()` lets a component load its own data. It runs a server function as the component renders,
and its answer becomes state:

```jsx
// search.goal
export server function search(q) {
  return db.fruit.filter((f) => f.includes(q));
}

export function Search() {
  var q = '';
  var found = call(search(q));

  return (
    <div>
      <input value={q} oninput={(e) => (q = e.target.value)} />
      <button onclick={found.reload}>Reload</button>
      {if (found.error) <p>{found.error}</p>
       else if (!found.value) <p>Loading…</p>
       else <ul class={found.loading ? 'dim' : ''}>{found.value.map((f) => <li key={f}>{f}</li>)}</ul>}
    </div>
  );
}
```

`found` is an object:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `value` | The answer: `undefined` until the first one arrives, then the latest. |
| `loading` | `true` while a request is on its way. The last value stays until the new one arrives. |
| `error` | `null`, or a message when the server function failed. The value it had stays. |
| `reload()` | Sends the request again, with the same arguments. |
| `cancel()` | Stops a request on its way, and keeps the value it had. |

How it runs:

- **On the server:** the call runs while the page renders, and the page is sent with the answer in
  it. Calls with the same function and arguments run once per page. A call whose arguments read
  another call's value runs after it; the others start together.
- **In the browser:** the page keeps that answer, so nothing is fetched when the page loads. When an
  argument (here `q`, which is state) changes, the call runs again. A newer request stops the one
  before it, so an old answer never replaces a new one. A component that first appears in the
  browser (in an `{if}`, say) sends its request as it renders.
- **Errors:** a failure on the server is logged and goes to
  [`onError`](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security#errors). The page shows the same message the browser would get,
  `server function /_m/<file>/<name> failed: 500`, and never the error's own details.
- **Cancel:** `cancel()` stops the request in the browser and drops its answer. The server may
  still finish the work.

The rules:

- `call()` goes at the top of a component, as `var name = call(load(args))`, with one server function
  call inside. Anywhere else it is a compile error.
- Don't assign the var: run the call again with `name.reload()`. A handler can set `name.value`, as
  when a server function already gives the new list: `found.value = addFruit(name)`.
- The code for `call()` is a small file of its own, and only components that use it load it.
- In a `#strict` file, `found.value` has the server function's return type, or `undefined`.
- A file that declares or imports its own `call` uses that one instead.

# Security

All of this is on with no setup. `goal.config.js`, at the top of the app folder, can change the parts
marked *config*:

```js
export default { csp: "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-{nonce}'", csrf: false, bodyLimit: 5_000_000 };
```

`goal build` copies it into `dist/server` with the server code, so it can import `.js` files of the
app's, and `goal start` reads it from there.

## Escaping

Every value is escaped in text and in attributes. There is no raw-HTML escape hatch. `<script>`,
`<style>`, `srcdoc` and string event handlers (`onclick="..."`) are compile errors. A file's CSS goes
in its [style block](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/components#styles), which `goal build` puts in a stylesheet of its own, so pages
need no inline styles.

## URLs

In `href`, `src`, `action`, `formaction` and the other URL attributes, only relative, `http(s):`,
`mailto:` and `tel:` URLs get through. A `javascript:` or `data:` URL written in the source is a
compile error. One that comes from data becomes `about:invalid#blocked`, on the server and when the
browser patches the page.

## Headers

Every response has:

- a strict Content-Security-Policy with a fresh nonce for the loader (*config* `csp`, where `{nonce}`
  is replaced, or `false` to send none);
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and `frame-ancestors 'none'`;
- same-origin opener and resource policies, a Referrer-Policy and a Permissions-Policy;
- HSTS over TLS.

## CSRF

A POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE from another site is refused: always when `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site`
says cross-site, and without `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` the request needs the CSRF token. Forms
that send data get the token as a hidden field automatically, server functions send it for you, and
your own `fetch` can send it as the `x-csrf-token` header (*config* `csrf: false` to turn it off).

Routes in a [`group /path api`](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/routes#api-routes) skip the check, because they neither read nor set
cookies: a request from another site carries nothing to misuse, and the route checks a token from a
header itself. Other sites' pages can read their answers only when *config* `cors` lists the site
(or is `'*'`), and never with cookies.

## Only what the browser needs

A component's root element carries its state and only the props its browser code reads. Props used
only while rendering on the server never reach the page.

## The rest

- A client may send 120 requests that change things (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, server functions
  included) a minute; more get 429 with `Retry-After` (*config* `rateLimit: { max, window }` in
  milliseconds, or `false`). Reading is never limited. Behind a proxy or load balancer every request
  seems to come from it, so set *config* `trustProxy: true` (or the number of proxies) to tell
  clients apart by `X-Forwarded-For`.
- Request bodies are limited to 1 MB (*config* `bodyLimit`).
- `redirect()` stays on this site unless told otherwise.
- Cookies are `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite=Lax` unless a route says otherwise.
- Static files are served only from `public/` and the chunks folder.
- Error details (the stack) are shown only in `goal dev`. Otherwise the page is a plain error page, and
  the error is logged.

## Errors

An error that a route or server function throws is logged, and answered with a 500 page. To report it
somewhere too, such as an error tracker, give `goal.config.js` an `onError` (*config*):

```js
import { report } from './report.js';

export default {
  onError(error, request) {
    report(error, { method: request.method, path: request.path });
  },
};
```

It runs after the answer is on its way, so it doesn't slow the page, and an error it throws is
logged. `goal add sentry` sets it up for [Sentry](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/tools).

# Types

A `.goal` file that starts with `#strict` is type-checked: goal.js finds wrong props, state of the
wrong type, markup that can't render and bad data sent to the server, before the app runs. Any other
file compiles as it always has.

```jsx
#strict
export type Note = { id: number, text: string, done?: boolean };

export function Board({ initial }: { initial: Note[] }) {
  var notes = initial;                // a Note[]: worked out from initial
  var draft: string | null = null;    // written: null alone doesn't say
  ...
}

export server function addNote(text: string): Note[] { ... }

route GET /notes/{id: number} { ... }
```

## Writing types

Types are written `name: Type`, in five places; everything else is worked out from the code.

1. A component's props, on its parameter.
2. A `var` whose initial value doesn't say its type, like `[]` or `null`.
3. A server function's parameters, and its result if you want it checked.
4. A route's path parameters: `{id: number}` matches only a number, and the route gets it as one.
5. `type` declarations, which `export` shares with other `.goal` files.

| Type | Written |
| --- | --- |
| Text, numbers, true or false, nothing | `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined` |
| A choice of values | `'draft' \| 'sent'`, `string \| null` |
| A list | `Note[]` |
| An object, with optional fields | `{ id: number, text: string, done?: boolean }` |
| A function, for function props | `(x: string) => void` |
| Markup, for children | `Markup` |
| Anything, unchecked | `unknown` |
| A declared type | `Note` |

## What is checked

| Check | Code | Error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A prop of the wrong type | `<Counter start="1" />` | `Counter's start is number, not string` |
| A required prop left out | `<Counter />` | `Counter needs start` |
| A prop the component doesn't take | `<Counter strat={1} />` | `Counter has no prop strat; did you mean start?` |
| State given the wrong type | `count = 'x'` | `count is number, not string` |
| Markup that can't render | `{user}` | `{ name: string } can't be rendered: render a field of it, like {user.name}` |
| A true-or-false attribute | `disabled={'no'}` | `disabled takes true or false, not string` |
| A call's arguments | `addNote(42)` | `addNote takes string, not number` |
| A returned value | `return 1` in a function typed `: string` | `f returns string, not number` |
| A server function's result | `: () => void` | `addNote's result travels as JSON: () => void can't` |

A `#strict` file must also give a type wherever one can't be worked out: a component's props, a server
function's parameters, a `var` that starts as `[]` or `null`, and a value from a `.js` module, which has
no types (`const rows: Note[] = db.all()`). What still can't be worked out is unknown, and unknown is
never an error.

## Imports

A `#strict` file can import `.js` modules and npm packages freely. Among `.goal` files it can import
only `#strict` ones, so the props, types and server functions it uses are all known:

```
A.goal:2:1: ./Card.goal isn't #strict: a #strict file can import only #strict .goal files
```

## At runtime

Types are erased: the browser code carries none. Two checks stay on the server, because their values
come from the network:

- A server function's typed parameters: a request whose arguments don't fit is answered 400 and never
  reaches the function.
- A route's typed path parameters: `/notes/abc` doesn't match `/notes/{id: number}`, so it gets a 404.

## Where errors show

- `goal check` checks every file and lists each file's first error; it exits 1 when there are any.
- `goal build` fails on a type error, like any compile error.
- `goal dev` and the [Vite plugin](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/vite) show it over the page until it's fixed.
- The VS Code extension underlines it as you type.

# How it works

1. **Parse.** goal.js reads `.goal` files with acorn, extended for `route` and `{if}`, and rewrites
   them into plain JavaScript and JSX: a route becomes an async function, and an `if` chain becomes
   ternaries. A position map sends errors back to the line and column in the `.goal` file.
2. **Compile.** Each file becomes a server module and, for every interactive component, a client
   chunk. The compiler finds which `let`s, `const`s and functions depend on state, and marks only the
   parts of the markup that do: `{...}` holes get comment markers, and attributes get an id. Everything
   else is plain HTML.
3. **Render on the server.** A component's root element carries its chunk's URL, its state and the
   props its browser code reads. The page inlines the loader (about 1 KB gzipped), with the CSP nonce,
   only if the page has events. A page with no events ships no JavaScript at all.
4. **Resume in the browser.** The loader listens for the page's events at the document. On the first
   event in a component, it loads that component's chunk: the component as written,
   `function Counter(state, props)`, whose `var`s start from the saved state. The loader runs the
   handlers on the event's path, saves the `var`s they changed, runs the body again, and patches only
   the bindings whose value changed. If a handler waits for a server function, it patches again when
   the server answers. The chunk starts loading on intent (pointer over, focus), so it's usually there
   before the click or the first key.

## One source for the server and the browser

A `.goal` file is compiled once, and that one compile makes all of its code: the server module that
renders the HTML, each component's browser chunk, and the file's render module, which renders
components again in the browser. So both sides follow the same rules:

- **The same checks.** A compile error stops the whole file. Nothing reaches the browser that the
  server would refuse, and nothing runs on the server that the browser couldn't render.
- **The same templates.** A keyed list's row is one template that the server renders and the browser
  patches with, and a component rendered again in the browser uses the server's own templates. The
  HTML the browser makes can't drift from the HTML the server sent.
- **The same safety.** Escaping, attributes and the URL check come from the same helpers on both
  sides, so a `javascript:` URL is blocked whether the server renders it or the browser patches it in.
- **The same component.** The browser runs the component's body as you wrote it, with the same `var`
  state and computed `let` and `const`, so its next render agrees with the server's first one.

What differs is on purpose: routes, server functions and what they import stay on the server, and the
page gets only the props its browser code reads. Types are checked when the app compiles, and the
server checks again, when the request comes in, what a server function or a typed route receives,
since a request can come from anywhere.

## Size

`goal build` prints the gzipped size of each client chunk and of the loader. Helpers that several
components share go in a chunk of their own, and the keyed-list code in another, loaded only by
components with a keyed list. The code for calling server functions, and for rendering a component
inside another in the browser, goes only to the components that do it. In the demo app, the
component chunks are 220 to 1251 B, the shared helpers 980 B, the keyed-list code 1190 B, and the
loader 1064 B. The files' style blocks are one stylesheet, 327 B there.

## Live updates in goal dev

`goal dev` builds again when a file changes and tells the open pages what changed, over a stream at
`/_goal/hmr`:

- **A stylesheet:** the page loads it again in place. So does a style block: after a change to
  one, the page loads the stylesheet of the style blocks again, as well as getting the new code.
- **Code**, a component's or the server's: the page asks the server for itself again, sending the
  state each component has now. The server renders the page with that state, and the new body takes
  the old one's place, keeping the scroll. The focused element keeps the focus, and an input its
  caret and selection: it's found by its place in its component, so it needs no `id`, unless the
  change put another kind of element there. The next event runs the new code, because a
  dev chunk's URL names its build. With PostCSS, the stylesheet loads again too, because Tailwind
  CSS makes it from the code.
- **A compile error:** it shows over the page until a build works again.

A page reloads instead when the new code listens for an event type the page doesn't yet, or when the
state is too big to send. None of this is in `goal build`.

## Debugging

The browser runs the component as you wrote it: the same top level (`var count = …`, your `const`s,
your functions by name), with only the `var`s starting from the saved state and the markup turned into
values.

- `goal dev` serves the chunks unminified, with source maps back to the `.goal` files, so the browser's
  debugger shows your source, and breakpoints and stack traces point at your lines. Server stack
  traces in `goal dev` point at the `.goal` files too.
- `goal build` minifies and ships no source maps, so the source stays on the server.

## Editor support

The repository's `editors/vscode` folder has a VS Code extension: highlighting for `.goal` files
(routes, server functions, `{if}` in markup) and the compiler's errors as you type. Its README says how
to install it.

# Performance

## js-framework-benchmark

goal.js has a keyed implementation of [js-framework-benchmark](https://github.com/krausest/js-framework-benchmark),
which passes the benchmark's keyed check. On one Mac, in headless Chrome, with all seven frameworks run
together on 25 November 2026, the geometric mean of the nine timed operations, as a ratio to vanillajs
(lower is faster), was:

| Framework | Ratio to vanillajs |
|---|---|
| vanillajs | 1.00 |
| **goal.js 0.1** | **1.07** |
| solid 1.9.3 | 1.12 |
| svelte 5.42.1 | 1.16 |
| vue 3.5.39 | 1.21 |
| react 19.2 (hooks) | 1.69 |
| qwik 1.20.2 | 3.60 |

goal.js was faster than vanillajs at removing a row (0.88), creating 10,000 rows (0.97) and selecting
a row (0.98). Its weakest result was the partial update (1.50). This is one run on one machine; the
benchmark's official results are run on other hardware.

### goal.js 0.8 against 0.1

Ratios move from run to run with the machine's load, so versions are compared in the same run. On 26
November 2026, with goal.js 0.1, goal.js 0.8 and vanillajs run together on an Apple M5 at a load
average of about 2:

| Operation | goal.js 0.1 | goal.js 0.8 |
|---|---|---|
| Create 1,000 rows | 1.07 | 1.07 |
| Replace all rows | 1.07 | 1.08 |
| Partial update | 1.16 | 1.18 |
| Select a row | 1.36 | 1.25 |
| Swap rows | 1.21 | 1.18 |
| Remove a row | 1.07 | 1.09 |
| Create 10,000 rows | 1.09 | 1.08 |
| Append 1,000 rows | 1.08 | 1.07 |
| Clear rows | 1.47 | 1.22 |
| **Geometric mean** | **1.17** | **1.13** |

Each figure is the ratio to vanillajs in that run. 0.8 clears and selects rows faster, and the rest is
the same within the run's noise. Its JavaScript is 4.0 kB compressed (3.3 kB in 0.1), for the features
added since: types, components rendered in the browser, scoped styles.

## A 100,000-row virtual list

The repository's `examples/virtual` is a virtual list of 100,000 rows whose structure differs from row
to row: a badge that comes and goes, tags of any length, a meter. Only the rows in view, and a few
around them, are in the page. In the same headless Chrome:

| Operation | goal.js's script, per operation | Event to patched DOM, median (p95) |
|---|---|---|
| Scroll by 3 rows | 0.066 ms | 0.6 ms (0.8 ms) |
| Jump to a random place, replacing every row | 0.062 ms | 1.3 ms (1.6 ms) |
| Update every row's values and some rows' structure | 0.064 ms | 1.0 ms (1.3 ms) |

These are goal.js 0.8 on 26 November 2026, the median of three runs, each within 5% of the others.
goal.js's own script is a few hundredths of a millisecond per operation; the rest of the time is
Chrome's style and layout. Against goal.js 0.1 in the same rounds, the script is about 10% more per
operation (0.056 to 0.062 ms there) and the whole operation the same within noise.

Over the memory cycles of 200 jumps, 12 updates and 300 scroll steps each, the JS heap stays at about
0.93 MB after a garbage collection, with the same 291 DOM nodes and 5 event listeners every time: no
memory leak.

## Measuring it yourself

In a clone of the repository:

```bash
npm install
npm run bench:virtual             # about 3 to 4 minutes
npm run bench:virtual -- --quick  # under a minute
```

It builds `examples/virtual`, serves it, and drives headless Chrome over the DevTools protocol, with no
extra dependency. For scroll steps, random jumps and updates it reports the time from the event to the
patched DOM and the main thread's CPU time per operation: script, style, layout and all tasks. CPU
time leaves out what other programs on the machine take, though a busy machine still slows Chrome
down: compare versions in the same session, one after the other, and more than once. For memory it repeats all three in cycles and
compares the JS heap, DOM nodes and event listeners after a garbage collection: growth from cycle to
cycle is a leak.

- `--cycles 12` runs more memory cycles.
- `--json results.json` also saves the numbers.
- `CHROME=/path/to/chrome` sets the browser if it isn't in `/Applications`.

# Vite

To work on a goal.js app inside Vite's dev server, add the plugin:

```js
// vite.config.js
import { goal } from 'goaljs/vite';

export default {
  plugins: [goal()],
};
```

```bash
npx vite
```

The app works as it does under `goal dev`:

- Vite serves its own modules and the `public/` folder. Every other request goes to the app's routes
  and server functions, with error details and all the [security defaults](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security).
- Each component's browser code is a Vite module, and so is the code a component renders other
  components from. The `.goal` files themselves are never served: their server code stays on the
  server.
- [Live updates](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/how-it-works#live-updates-in-goal-dev) work the same way. A stylesheet change
  applies in place, a code change updates the page with each component's state kept, and a compile
  error shows over the page.
- With a `postcss.config.js`, the stylesheets in `public/` go through PostCSS, as they do in
  `goal dev`, and the app's `.env` is read into `process.env` (see [Tools](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/tools)).
- The files' [style blocks](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/components#styles) are one stylesheet, `/_goal/style.css`, which each
  page links.
- [Vitest](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/tools) uses the plugin too, so tests can import `.goal` files.

The plugin is for development. For production, build and serve the app with `goal build` and
`goal start`.

## Options

`goal({ config })` takes what `goal.config.js` would hold, such as `{ csrf: false }` or a CSP of your
own. See [Security](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security).

# Tools

`goal add` sets a tool up in an app: it installs the packages with npm and writes the config and glue
the tool needs, so it works with `.goal` files from the first run.

```bash
npx goal add tailwindcss          # in the app's folder
npx goal add prisma my-app        # or name the folder
npx goal add                      # lists the tools
```

| Tool | `goal add` | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/docs) | `tailwindcss` (4 or 3) | Classes from your `.goal` files compiled into `/style.css` |
| [PostCSS](https://postcss.org) | `postcss` | The stylesheets in `public/` run through PostCSS plugins, autoprefixer first |
| [Prisma](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm) | `prisma` | SQLite, a schema with a `Note` model, and `db.js` for server code |
| [Drizzle](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/overview) | `drizzle` | SQLite, a `notes` table in `db/schema.js`, and `db/index.js` for server code |
| [ESLint](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/) | `eslint` | `npm run lint` for `.js` and `.goal` files |
| [Prettier](https://prettier.io/docs/) | `prettier` | `npm run format` for `.js`, `.css`, `.json` and `.md` files |
| [Vitest](https://vitest.dev/guide/) | `vitest` | `npm test`, with tests that import `.goal` files |
| [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/docs/intro) | `playwright` | `npm run test:e2e`: Chromium against the built app |
| [Sentry](https://docs.sentry.io/platforms/javascript/guides/node/) | `sentry` | Errors from routes and server functions reported to Sentry |

When it's done, `goal add` says what it did and what to do next:

```
tailwindcss: the recipe for tailwindcss 4
  $ npm install --save-dev tailwindcss@4.3.5 @tailwindcss/postcss@4.3.5 postcss@8.5.33
  created postcss.config.js
  added to public/style.css: @import "tailwindcss" source("..");
  added to .gitignore: node_modules, dist
Next:
  - Link the stylesheet from your pages: <link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css" />
  ...
```

## What it changes

- **Nothing of yours is overwritten.** A file that's already there is kept, and `goal add` prints the
  recipe's version of it, so you can merge the two. A line a file already has, such as `dist` in
  `.gitignore` or `DATABASE_URL=` in `.env`, isn't added again. A script that's already in
  `package.json` is kept, except the placeholder `test` script that `npm init` writes.
- **Packages you have stay as they are.** The version you have also picks the recipe: an app on
  Tailwind CSS 3 gets the setup for 3. To ask for one, name it: `goal add tailwindcss@3`.
- **Each recipe installs the versions it was tested with.** npm saves them as `^` ranges, as it always
  does.
- **`package.json` gets `"type": "module"`.** Tools load their config files as ES modules, the way
  goal.js writes them. (`goal build` marks its own output as ES modules either way.)

## Notes on each tool

**Tailwind CSS and PostCSS.** When an app has a `postcss.config.js`, `goal dev` and `goal build` run
every stylesheet in `public/` through it, and the stylesheet of the files'
[style blocks](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/components#styles) too, and so does the [Vite plugin](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/vite). PostCSS and its plugins
come from the app's own `node_modules`. Tailwind CSS finds its classes in your `.goal` files. In
`goal dev`, a class you add to a `.goal` file is styled as soon as you save it, without a reload.

**Prisma and Drizzle.** Both use SQLite, with the database file named in `.env`. `goal dev`,
`goal start` and the Vite plugin read the app's `.env` into `process.env`, and a variable that's
already set in the environment wins. The database is used from server code only: a route or a
server function, where `await` is allowed.

```jsx
import { db } from './db.js';

export server function addNote(text) {
  await db.note.create({ data: { text } });
  return db.note.findMany();
}
```

**ESLint.** `goaljs/eslint` lets ESLint read `.goal` files. Each problem is reported at its place in
the `.goal` file, and `eslint --fix` fixes them there.

**Prettier.** Prettier doesn't format `.goal` files yet, so it leaves them alone.

**Vitest.** Tests import components and server functions from `.goal` files, through goal.js's
[Vite plugin](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/vite). A component called as a function renders its HTML:

```js
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Counter } from './Counter.goal';

test('Counter renders its start', () => {
  expect(String(Counter({ start: 41 }))).toContain('41');
});
```

**Playwright.** The tests run against the app as `goal build` and `goal start` serve it, with all the
[security headers](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security). The example test fails on any console error, which includes a script
or style the Content-Security-Policy blocks.

**Sentry.** `goal.config.js` gets an `onError` hook (see [Security](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security#errors)) that reports each
error to Sentry. Nothing is sent until `SENTRY_DSN` is set in `.env` or the environment.

## Recipes

Each tool's setup is a recipe: a file in the repository's
[recipes/](https://github.com/goallabs/goal/tree/main/recipes) folder, with one entry for each range
of the tool's versions. When a tool releases a version that needs a different setup, a pull request
adds an entry for it, and the tool's maintainers are welcome to send it. The folder's README covers
writing and testing a recipe.
